#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The core implementation for KEP-4832, moving the part making API calls to goroutine inside the preemption.

I confirmed that this feature:
- makes the latency of PostFilter 1/5 
  - This is when each preemption preempts 3 Pods. The more Pods to kill, the bigger the improvement is, vice versa.
- improves the throughput by double in the scenario of `PreemptionAsync` with multiple runs of scheduler-perf.

See: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128170#issuecomment-2439369996

---

The note on the implementation detail:

**About Activate()**

The preemption plugin moves the preemptor pod to activeQ when the goroutine fails.

This is because if, for example, the deletion API fails and no Pod/Delete happens, 
the preemptor Pod could get stuck at the unsched pod pool. (since no event moves the Pod)

For this operation, we reuse the existing `Activate()` method on the queue that moves the Pod from unsched to activeQ.
And, to address the case where the goroutine fails immediately and the preemptor pod hasn't come back to the queue yet, we utilize in-flight event and `moveRequestCycle` like we do with cluster events.

review_comments: Is there a way to make sure this list is update whenever a new event is added?

Since we use Activate, can we rely on it to trigger requeue in all scenarios (not only in error case)? In such case we would simplify the code and could send all delete requestes including the last one in one loop. The `delete(ev.preempting, pod.UID)` could be in defer clause.

In async version, preemption failures does not prevent scheduler from annotating pod as unschedulable and setting nominated node (in `handleSchedulingFailure`). Isn't there a risk that the pod will remain unschedulable forever?
Good point, I implemented `PodActivator` to deal with the failure scenario; we move the preemptor to activeQ when the preemption goroutine fails

Not sure yet how the activator works, but I was thinking about something simpler. What about setting error status in `preempting` which would be read the next time the PreEnque is called?

Maybe I'm missing something obvious, but I've just noticed that the plugin does not register to any cluster events. I don't see us calling `moveToActiveQ` either, so how was it supposed to be unblocked?

> What about setting error status in preempting which would be read the next time the PreEnque is called?

The problem here is, for example, when the preemption API calls aren't successful at all, the preemptor Pod gets stuck in the unschedulable pod pool because no Pod/Delete event happens.
So, we have to somehow let the preemption plugin move the Pod out of the unsched pod pool. That's `Activate()`.

> Maybe I'm missing something obvious, but I've just noticed that the plugin does not register to any cluster events. I don't see us calling moveToActiveQ either, so how was it supposed to be unblocked?

We don't need to register any events in the preemption plugin because the preemptor Pod should have the other plugins in unschedulablePlugins.

For example, the pod is originally rejected by the node resource fit,
1. the preemptor pod gets `unschedulablePlugin: node-resource-fit`
2. the scheduling queue tries to requeue this pod every time node-resource-fit's QHint returns Queue, but the preemption plugin blocks the requeueing at PreEnqueue until all the preemption is done.
3. When the last pod is deleted, the scheduling queue, again, should tries to requeue the preemptor pod, and this requeueing goes through because the preemption plugin doesn't block this pod anymore at PreEnqueue.

That's how it works

> We don't need to register any events in the preemption plugin because the preemptor Pod should have the other plugins in unschedulablePlugins.
> 
Isn't it something https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127180 is going to change, so that only the GatedPlugin's events are supposed to be checked? Here we don't register any, but I think it's possible that preemption plugin will become the gated one. Note that `runPreEnqueuePlugins` can reassign to the preemption plugin, as it become a blocking one (for instance when resource-fit let the pod go for some other reason).

BTW. why we need `preempting` map then if we wait for 'resource-fit' plugin anyway?

> Isn't it something https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127180 is going to change

Good point, Yes correct. Once that change comes, my assumption would break. Let me register Pod/delete event in the preemption plugin.

> BTW. why we need preempting map then if we wait for 'resource-fit' plugin anyway?

Because we want to wait for all API calls of the preemption to be completed and then try to schedule the preemptor pod again.
If we didn't do this, let's say there are 5 victims, the preemptor could be requeued to activeQ with the first pod's deletion, while the other 4 Pods are still alive.
Note that it will be moved to the backoff queue, so it's one more argument why we should do this only in error case (I guess in the non-error case we'd rather prefer to move it to active directly).

One more thought. Note that the removed low priority pods won't be able to jump again in this spot until the pod times out in the backoff queue. I guess it's not bad, as this place will stay reserved when the pod is retried.

I however have a different question. If some pod changes the nominated node name, is there an event that can wake up pods waiting for such a change? In our case, the removed low priority pods may remain unschedulable in case the preempted pod got eventually scheduled in different location, in which they couldn't due to other constraints. I know it's a bit theoretical and we have flush mechanism, but still.

> I guess in the non-error case we'd rather prefer to move it to active directly

This is a good topic to discuss. (no need to block this PR though)
In the theory that we've had so far, backoffQ is the _**penalty**_ that the pod wasted the scheduling cycle.
So, the point would be whether we should treat the scheduling cycle that has triggered the preemption as "it was wasted" or "it was necessary".

The rough idea that I have is like:
- When calculating the victims on the node, we assume the nominated Pods are on the node already.
  - Lower priority nominated Pods could be selected as victims, while higher ones shouldn't.
- Then, if lower nominated Pods are selected, `prepareCandidate` (or `prepareCandidateAsync`) unnominates them instead of deleting them.

So, in short, the nominated info on lower pods will be un-nominated only when necessary.

But, apart from that idea, I'd like to still seek the simplest option like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128067. 
We have to think thoroughly if there's any corner case though, maybe we can just do that.

It would be good to consider how Autoscaler handles nominated node before taking the decision to remove this logic. If some of the low priority pods no longer fit the nominated node, Autoscaler should be aware that it needs to still consider them in simulation in other places, but not necessarily tied to this particular node, which would be overallocated.

Another argument for keeping this logic is that such overallocation would block scheduling of even lower priority pods which could fit. If unominated pods still fit, they could be still scheduled in the same place. The only worry is potentially unnecessary ongoing preemptions would be wasted and the risk unnominated pods won't reschedule, but not sure about it yet.

> What about setting error status in preempting which would be read the next time the PreEnque is called?

The problem here is, for example, when the preemption API calls aren't successful at all, the preemptor Pod gets stuck in the unschedulable pod pool because no Pod/Delete event happens.
So, we have to somehow let the preemption plugin move the Pod out of the unsched pod pool. That's `Activate()`.

> Maybe I'm missing something obvious, but I've just noticed that the plugin does not register to any cluster events. I don't see us calling moveToActiveQ either, so how was it supposed to be unblocked?

We don't need to register any events in the preemption plugin because the preemptor Pod should have the other plugins in unschedulablePlugins.

For example, the pod is originally rejected by the node resource fit,
1. the preemptor pod gets `unschedulablePlugin: node-resource-fit`
2. the scheduling queue tries to requeue this pod every time node-resource-fit's QHint returns Queue, but the preemption plugin blocks the requeueing at PreEnqueue until all the preemption is done.
3. When the last pod is deleted, the scheduling queue, again, should tries to requeue the preemptor pod, and this requeueing goes through because the preemption plugin doesn't block this pod anymore at PreEnqueue.

That's how it works

Good point, Yes correct. Once that change comes, my assumption would break. Let me register Pod/delete event in the preemption plugin.

> BTW. why we need preempting map then if we wait for 'resource-fit' plugin anyway?

Because we want to wait for all API calls of the preemption to be completed and then try to schedule the preemptor pod again.
If we didn't do this, let's say there are 5 victims, the preemptor could be requeued to activeQ with the first pod's deletion, while the other 4 Pods are still alive.
